title: Living his calm
hookLine: detachment here means love without clutching
last: FIFTEEN RAGAS — A RAGA OF HIS OWN.

lines: THE LOVE IS IN THE LOOSENING.
cards: A parent is teaching a child to ride a bike, running alongside with one hand on the back of the seat. At some point the hand has to come off, a little at a time. Grip too tight and the child never learns to balance.
Let go too soon and they fall. The love is in the loosening. All week, Guru Tegh Bahadur has been saying the world is passing.
So should we love it less?

teach.b: In Sikh teaching, detachment doesn't mean running away. It's a householder's path.
Guru Tegh Bahadur was married to Mata Gujri, and was father to the boy who became Guru Gobind Singh.

Tradition remembers long years of quiet meditation at Bakala, and he still lived in a family, traveled, founded the town that became Anandpur, and in the end went to Delhi, where Sikhs remember he gave his life for others.
So when his hymns say the world is passing, the point isn't to stop caring. Look at the week. The steady one in Sorath sees gold and dust alike, and merges with the Lord like water into water.
The friends who leave in hard times were loving their own comfort. The scent is in the flower, not in the forest. Remembering is the real work, and life without it slips by.
Put them together and you get a love that holds without gripping.

teach.h: THE LOTUS IN WATER STAYS DRY.
teach.b: Guru Nanak gave Sikhs the picture for it: a lotus that grows in water but stays dry, a duck that swims all day and isn't soaked.
Those are the images Sikhs reach for when they talk about living in the world without drowning in it.

teach.h: THE OPEN HAND LETS LOVE STAY.
teach.b: Love without clutching isn't loving less.
It's loving without needing to own. You can cherish your children and still let them become who they are. You can enjoy your home and not fall apart when the roof leaks.
The calm in the ninth Guru's hymns isn't distance. It's the open hand that lets love stay.

how: The Sikh path is a householder's path, with work and family, and Sikhs describe the Gurus' ideal as staying unattached in the world like a lotus in water; Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns are often sung as reminders of that steady, open love.

o: a lotus, dry in the water it grows in
a garland of flowers for a guest
a lamp lit before the scripture

games.q: living his calm — tap the pairs.

s: in Sikh teaching, detachment means leaving your family
the Sikh path is a householder's path; detachment means love without clutching.
Guru Tegh Bahadur was a husband and father
married to Mata Gujri, and father of Guru Gobind Singh.
the lotus image pictures living in the world without drowning in it
it grows in water and stays dry.

games.q: the hymns keep saying the world is passing. what does that mean for the people you love?
o: love them less, so it hurts less.
love them with an open hand, without clutching.
leave them and go to the forest.
games.why: Sikh detachment isn't distance. like the lotus that grows in water but stays dry, it's love that holds without gripping.

practice: Bring to mind someone you love deeply, and notice any place where love has turned into gripping: worry about their choices, a need for them to call, a fear of losing them.
Without scolding yourself, open your hands in your lap, palms up, and hold them in mind the way that parent's hand rests on the bike seat, there but light, wishing them well exactly as they are.
If you pray, you can place them in Waheguru's care.

wordCard.voice: Kamal, lotus. In Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns, detachment means love without clutching: living in the world like a kamal in water.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: kamal, lotus. Gurbani's picture of living in the world, in the water but not soaked.

carryVoice: Your line: love without clutching. Like a lotus: in the water, and not drowned by it. That's day five hundred eighty-eight.
